overview: Foley Wines is a New Zealand-listed, vertically integrated premium wine producer operating six wineries and a distillery across Marlborough (Grove Mill, Vavasour), Martinborough (Martinborough Vineyard, Te Kairanga, Lighthouse Gin) and Central Otago (Mt Difficulty), supplemented by cellar-door/hospitality venues including The Runholder. It sells bottled wine domestically and to export markets (USA, UK/Europe, Australia, Asia/Pacific) under a 'premiumisation' strategy that avoids the commodity bulk-wine market. The company is majority controlled by US businessman William P Foley II (Fidelity National Financial/Cannae founder) through Foley Holdings New Zealand Limited and personal holdings, making it a controlled micro-cap with limited free float and heavy related-party dealing.

business_model.summary: Revenue comes from bottled wine sales through wholesale/distributor channels in export markets and direct/retail channels domestically, plus a smaller hospitality/cellar-door and bulk-wine/spirits/merchandise revenue line. The company owns vineyards and wineries (capital intensive, long inventory-ageing cycles) rather than solely contract-sourcing grapes, giving it control over quality but exposing it to biological-asset fair-value swings, vineyard revaluations and harvest variability. FY2025 total revenue was NZ$70.582m (bottled wine sales NZ$66.375m, up 6% on record case sales of 610,000 9L cases, +9% YoY); H1 FY2026 (six months to 31 Dec 2025) revenue was NZ$34.916m, bottled sales NZ$32.490m (+0.5%) on case sales of 290,000 (down 2%). Management treats 'operating earnings' (profit before interest, impairment and IAS 41 revaluation gains/losses) as the key internal metric because IAS 41 fair-value movements on harvested grapes are non-cash and simply reverse between the harvest year and the sale year.
business_model.customer_type: B2B distributor/wholesale for export markets plus B2C retail, cellar-door and hospitality domestically; not a bulk/commodity supplier by strategy
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2025 bottled case sales: New Zealand 170,000 cases (28%, -4%), UK/Europe 144,000 (24%, +8%), USA 115,000 (19%, -14%), Australia 103,000 (17%, +27%), Asia/Pacific 73,000 (12%, +115%), Rest of World 5,000 (1%, +67%); total 610,000 cases, export cases +14.6% vs total NZ wine export market -7.1%. H1 FY2026: NZ 82,000 (-10%), UK/Europe 89,000 (+19%), Australia 46,000 (-18%), USA 45,000 (-4%), Asia/Pacific 26,000 (+8%); total 290,000 (-2%).

main_competitors: Numerous independent Marlborough/Central Otago producers amid a fragmented, oversupplied industry
competitive_position.market_position: Small-cap, multi-region premium portfolio player (~NZ$70m revenue) versus much larger scaled competitors (Delegat, Constellation, Pernod Ricard, Indevin) with far greater balance sheet strength and bulk/contract flexibility; FWL's stated edge is a multi-region 'one-stop' brand portfolio (Marlborough, Martinborough, Central Otago) that lets distributors source varied varietals and price points from one supplier.

moat_factors.description: Six recognised regional brands spanning three acclaimed wine regions gives distribution partners a broader assortment than single-region rivals; consistent wine-show medals and 90+ point critic scores support premium positioning.

Vertical integration (vineyards + wineries + cellar doors) gives quality control and asset backing (NTA/share NZ$1.64 vs NZ$0.50 share price) but ties up capital and cannot flex down quickly when demand falls.

Management cites 'strong distribution partnerships' in UK and Asia (China) and cross-supply deals with related party Foley Family Wines Inc. in the US as a source of resilience versus a shrinking overall NZ export market.

Refusing to dump into the bulk-wine glut protects brand value but means FWL absorbs inventory carrying costs and promotional spend rather than clearing stock, and it still cannot avoid industry-wide price competition on branded product.

weaknesses: Sub-scale relative to major NZ wine groups (Delegat, Indevin, Constellation) with less bargaining power on grape sourcing, freight and retailer listing fees
Illiquid NZX micro-cap (~NZ$33m market cap at NZ$0.50/share) with a controlling shareholder holding ~66.5%, leaving a thin free float and wide bid/ask spreads
High fixed-cost, capital-intensive vineyard/winery asset base that cannot be quickly resized when the industry cycle turns down
Earnings quality distorted year to year by non-cash IAS 41 biological-asset revaluations and periodic property revaluation write-downs
Heavy reliance on promotional/A&P spend to defend volume in an oversupplied, discount-driven market, compressing margins even when case sales grow

growth_drivers: Premiumisation strategy continuing to take share in a shrinking market — FY2025 export case sales +14.6% vs total NZ wine exports -7.1%; Asia/Pacific case sales +115% FY2025 and China identified as a 'major focus' with strong demand across all three regions/varietals
UK/Europe momentum (+8% FY2025 cases, +19% H1 FY2026) via strong distribution partnerships

Hospitality/brand-home expansion (The Runholder in Martinborough, Mt Difficulty Cellar Door and Restaurant) building direct-to-consumer margin, event/wedding revenue and brand equity; Toast Martinborough festival returning to The Runholder annually from November 2026

Vineyard replanting programme improving varietal mix and reducing third-party grape dependence, with the bulk of that redevelopment now largely complete (management flagged a pause after two more areas)

Potential industry-wide recovery as the global oversupply cycle eventually rebalances (structural but slow, ~1-2%/yr demand growth expected by industry bodies) — any recovery in bulk/grape pricing and reduced discounting would be a strong operating leverage tailwind given FWL's largely fixed cost base
Debt reduction focus (net loans and borrowings down from NZ$52.5m at FY2024 to NZ$40.6m at FY2025 to NZ$37.6m at H1 FY2026) freeing future cash flow from interest costs as rates ease

business.risk: Structural NZ/global wine oversupply and price competition
business.description: Large 2022/2023/2025 Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc harvests created a persistent industry glut; 2024 broker offers of surplus bulk Sauvignon Blanc as low as $2.15/litre; the 2026 harvest update (29 May 2026) reported a smaller crop than the prior year, and preliminary indications are the 2026 Marlborough grape price will be ~20% lower than the FY2025 average of $1,812/tonne — the stock fell 8.5% to NZ$0.43 on that announcement.

Central Otago experienced disruptive weather and an early frost in the 2024/25 growing season, cutting regional yield and driving a NZ$1,317,000 unrealised fair-value loss on harvested grapes in FY2025; the FY2024 harvest fell 21% to 6,404 tonnes versus FY2023's 8,137 tonnes.

business.risk: Export market concentration and channel dependence
business.description: USA case sales fell 14% in FY2025 and a further 4% in H1 FY2026; Australia fell 18% in H1 FY2026 after a strong FY2025; New Zealand domestic sales fell 10% in H1 FY2026 amid weak discretionary retail spending.

Extensive related-party dealings with Foley Family Wines Inc. (US distributor, 33.33% owner of the FWL parent's majority shareholder), Wharekauhau Country Estate (74.6% Foley-owned lodge), Foley Hospitality Ltd (100% Foley-owned) and Lighthouse Distillery Ltd (part-owned by a former FWL director) create potential conflicts of interest, though all are disclosed.

financial.description: Total loans and borrowings (excl. convertible note and leases) were NZ$37.6m at 31 Dec 2025 against operating EBITDA that fell from NZ$16.2m (FY2024) to NZ$12.6m (FY2025); the FY2025 year required NZ$47.5m drawn and NZ$58.8m repaid as facilities were refinanced, evidencing active balance-sheet management under pressure. Interest expense (NZ$3.6m FY2025) remains a material drag on a small operating base.

financial.risk: Convertible note and near-term bank facility renewal
financial.description: A NZ$10.9m related-party convertible note (held by Foley Holdings New Zealand Limited) sits in current liabilities, and the BNZ banking facility renewed in August 2023 for a 3-year term is due for renewal around August 2026 — a near-term refinancing event for a company that reported a net loss in FY2025.

A NZ$4,607,000 property revaluation decrement (mainly the Te Kairanga/Runholder site) drove the FY2025 headline net loss of NZ$(1.857)m despite positive operating earnings; IAS 41 biological-asset fair-value swings (loss of NZ$1,317,000 in FY2025, loss of NZ$3,458,000 in FY2024) add further non-cash noise that can mislead investors reading only headline NPAT.

No final dividend was paid for FY2024 (NPAT collapsed to a loss); a 2.0 cents per share fully imputed final dividend resumed for FY2025 (paid October 2025, NZ$1.315m), but the Board has explicitly prioritised debt reduction over distributions while conditions remain tough.

regulatory.description: The US is NZ wine's largest export market (~NZ$762m of exports, over one-third of total NZ wine export earnings, year to June 2025). A 10% reciprocal tariff took effect 5 April 2025, rising to 15% in August 2025, and a further Section 122 adjustment took the tariff to 12.5% from 24 July 2026 — bringing the total effective US tariff on NZ wine and spirits to roughly 17% (including the pre-existing ~4.5% MFN rate) as of 2026. Wine was not among the NZ products (e.g., beef, kiwifruit) granted exemptions. FWL's H1 FY2026 accounts already show NZ$204,000 of related-party discounts specifically attributed to the new US tariffs.

Excise duty and HPA (Health Promotion Agency) levy costs NZ$3,054,000 in H1 FY2026 (NZ$6,135,000 FY2025) are a direct, non-negotiable cost line; further increases in NZ or export-market alcohol excise/duty would compress margins.

macro.risk: Consumer downtrading and declining alcohol consumption
macro.description: Global and NZ per-capita wine consumption has been declining, particularly among younger demographics, compounding the industry oversupply; total NZ packaged wine market volumes were down 7.1% in the year to June 2025.

Revenue is earned in USD, GBP, EUR and AUD against an NZD cost base (vineyards, wineries, NZ payroll); FX movements directly affect reported NZD revenue and margin, and forward FX contracts already generated a NZ$743,000 unrealised loss in H1 FY2026.

As a leveraged capital-intensive producer, FWL benefits directly from NZ interest rate declines (management cited 'lower interest rates' as a factor reducing H1 FY2026 finance costs) but remains exposed if rates were to rise again.

International shipping delays were cited as affecting H1 FY2026 trade receivables timing; glass, packaging and insurance costs have been rising, partially offset by the 'super lightweight' bottle transition.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The NZ wine industry, and Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc in particular, is working through a structural oversupply built up over the large 2022, 2023 and 2025 harvests, compounded by softening global demand since COVID. Industry commentary (2025-2026) describes a 'prolonged downturn' with growers cutting production, vines being removed, and a rebuild expected to take years at only 1-2% annual demand growth rather than a quick snapback. FWL's own 29 May 2026 harvest update reported a smaller 2026 crop than 2025 and a preliminary ~20% decline in the Marlborough grape price.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — agricultural production cycle (weather-dependent annual harvest) layered on top of a multi-year industry destocking cycle and consumer-discretionary demand sensitivity
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high given leverage (~NZ$37.6m bank debt plus NZ$10.9m convertible note plus ~NZ$11.5m lease liabilities against NZ$142.98m equity at Dec 2025)

recent_developments.event: 2026 harvest result announcement: crop smaller than the prior year and preliminary 2026 Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc grape price indicated ~20% below the FY2025 average of NZ$1,812/tonne; shares fell 8.5% to NZ$0.43 on the news.

H1 FY2026 (six months to 31 Dec 2025) result released: revenue NZ$34.916m, operating earnings NZ$2.649m (+30.2%), reported NPAT NZ$2.300m (+112%), operating EBITDA NZ$7.607m (down 3.8%), operating cash flow NZ$6.709m (down 39% YoY on receivables timing and higher promotional spend); early indications for the 2026 harvest were then for yields in line with historic averages.

Annual Shareholders Meeting held at The Runholder, Martinborough; William P Foley II stood for election as a Non-Independent Director (having rejoined the Board 24 January 2025 after his son Robert P Foley II resigned) and was elected with only ~90.96% support (~8.6% against/withheld), a notable minority protest vote for a controlling shareholder's board seat; the NZ Shareholders' Association separately recommended voting against long-tenured (12+ year) director Tony Anselmi on board-renewal grounds.

FY2025 annual report published: revenue NZ$70.582m (+6%), record case sales of 610,000 (+9%, export cases +14.6% vs total NZ export market -7.1%), operating earnings NZ$1.388m (down from NZ$4.129m FY2024), operating EBITDA NZ$12.628m (down 22%), net loss after tax NZ$(1.857)m (vs NZ$(4.081)m FY2024, which included a one-off NZ$4.548m deferred tax charge from lost building depreciation), a NZ$4.607m property revaluation decrement (largely the Te Kairanga/Runholder site), and resumption of a final dividend of 2.0 cents per share fully imputed after paying no dividend for FY2024.
CEO Mark Turnbull departed after 13 years in the role (announced February 2025); Mike Higgins (previously CFO/Interim CEO) became CEO, with Jane Trought as CFO.

US tariffs on NZ wine imports progressively increased: 10% reciprocal tariff from 5 April 2025, raised to 15% in August 2025, then a Section 122 rate change to 12.5% from 24 July 2026, taking the total effective US duty on NZ wine to roughly 17% including the ~4.5% MFN base rate — directly affecting FWL's largest single export market.

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 result (27 February 2026) and 2026 Harvest Result (29 May 2026)

items.target: Initially guided in line with historic averages (Feb 2026); revised down (29 May 2026) to smaller than the prior year's harvest
items.notes: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc grape price preliminarily indicated ~20% below FY2025's average of NZ$1,812/tonne

items.target: Approximately NZ$4.5m for FY2026, in line with the two-year average and below depreciation, focused on Central Otago vineyard development/frost protection and an urgent Vavasour winery wastewater treatment upgrade
items.notes: Guided in the FY2025 annual report; H1 FY2026 actual capex of NZ$1.351m tracking below the prior comparative period (NZ$1.894m)

items.target: No explicit forward dividend target; Board states it will evaluate cash flow, sustainable operating earnings and capital requirements each period, with continued priority on reducing debt over the next 12 months
items.notes: FY2025 final dividend of 2.0 cps resumed after a nil FY2024 final; no explicit numeric guidance given for FY2026 dividends

items.target: No quantitative revenue/earnings guidance issued; management describes 2026 as continuing to face 'headwinds in the global economy' and a persistent global wine oversupply impacting pricing and margins, while expressing confidence in the premiumisation strategy and distribution partnerships
items.notes: August 2026 annual report and November 2026 AGM are the next scheduled disclosure events per the H1 FY2026 shareholder calendar

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Mike Higgins: 'It has been a very challenging period for the broader industry both domestically and globally... We are seeing significant volumes of bulk Sauvignon Blanc on the market at very low prices, which has added to the aggressive price competition in the market for branded wine... Bulk wine has never been a sales strategy for us.' On the 2026 harvest: 'The market price for Sauvignon Blanc grapes in Marlborough is down on last year's average grape price of $1,812 per tonne and preliminary indications are that the price for the 2026 vintage is going to be approximately 20% lower.'

bull_case: Premiumisation strategy is demonstrably taking share in a shrinking market: FY2025 export case sales +14.6% versus the total NZ wine export market -7.1%, with especially strong momentum in Asia/Pacific (+115% FY2025) and UK/Europe (+8% FY2025, +19% H1 FY2026)

H1 FY2026 profitability improved sharply (operating earnings +30.2%, reported NPAT +112% YoY) even as the industry remained under pressure, suggesting the worst of the FY2024/25 margin compression may be behind the company

Asset-backed valuation support: net tangible assets of NZ$1.64/share versus a NZ$0.50 share price implies a very large discount to book, with owned vineyards, wineries and hospitality venues (The Runholder, Mt Difficulty Cellar Door) providing tangible collateral
Active deleveraging (loans and borrowings down from ~NZ$52.5m FY2024 to ~NZ$40.6m FY2025 to ~NZ$37.6m H1 FY2026) reduces interest costs and financial risk into any industry recovery

A structural, multi-year industry destocking cycle implies eventual rebalancing; any recovery in grape/bulk pricing and reduced promotional discounting would flow through with significant operating leverage given FWL's largely fixed vineyard/winery cost base
bear_case: The core NZ wine industry problem (structural Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc oversupply) is not resolved and, per the 29 May 2026 harvest update, grape prices are still falling (~20% lower than FY2025) even as the crop itself shrank — this is a demand problem, not just a supply problem, and industry voices expect only 1-2%/year rebuild rather than a snapback

US tariffs (progressively raised to an effective ~17% by mid-2026) directly hit FWL's largest export market at the worst possible time, adding cost pressure that is already showing up as related-party tariff discounts in the accounts

Governance and liquidity structure is a persistent overhang: William P Foley II and Foley Holdings New Zealand Limited control roughly two-thirds of the register, leaving a thin free float, an illiquid NZX micro-cap (~NZ$33m market cap), extensive related-party transactions, and a board where a controlling shareholder's own re-election drew a meaningful ~8.6% protest vote in November 2025

Earnings quality is volatile and hard to read headline-to-headline: FY2025's net loss was driven by a NZ$4.6m non-cash property revaluation decrement and IAS 41 grape fair-value swings on top of genuinely weaker operating earnings (down from NZ$10.2m FY2023 to NZ$4.1m FY2024 to NZ$1.4m FY2025), and the dividend has already been cut to zero once (FY2024) in this downturn

Balance sheet still carries meaningful debt (~NZ$37.6m bank debt plus a NZ$10.9m related-party convertible note classified as a current liability) against a depressed and cyclical earnings base, with the BNZ banking facility due for renewal around August 2026 — a near-term refinancing risk in a still-difficult trading environment
